Football Hall of Fame]] |language=en}}</ref> At age 36, Sanders became the second-youngest player to be inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Jonathan |date=July 29, 2022 |title=Niners training camp 2022: Bump in road at practice won't slow Trey Lance's roll, plus Deebo deal on horizon |url=https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/niners-training-camp-2022-bump-in-road-at-practice-wont-slow-trey-lances-roll-plus-deebo-deal-on-horizon/ |access-date=July 31, 2022 |website=CBSSports.com |language=en}}</ref> In 2019, Sanders was named to the [[National Football League 100th Anniversary All-Time Team|NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFL 100 |url=https://www.nfl.com/100/all-time-team/roster |access-date=March 5, 2022 |website=www.nfl.com |publisher=[[National Football League]] |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2007, he was ranked by [[NFL Network]]'s ''[[NFL Top 10]]'' series as the most elusive runner in NFL history, and in 2012 was placed No. 1 on their list of the greatest players to never play in a Super Bowl.<ref name="NFL Top 10 Elusive Runners">{{cite web |author=NFL Network |date=May 28, 2008 |title=Top 10 most elusive runners in NFL history |url=http://www.nfl.com/nflnetwork/story/09000d5d8087474a/article/top-10-most-elusive-runners-in-nfl-history |access-date=September 9, 2013 |website=www.nfl.com |publisher=[[National Football League]]}}</ref><ref name="NFL Top 10 Superbowl Miss">{{Cite web |date=January 30, 2012 |title=Some all-time great players never even reached Super Bowl |url=http://www.nfl.com/superbowl/story/09000d5d8267672f/article/some-alltime-great-players-never-even-reached-super-bowl |access-date=September 9, 2013 |website=NFL.com |publisher=[[National Football League]]}}</ref>

Sanders led the NFL in rushing yards four times (second to Brown), and in rushing touchdowns once in 1994. He co-won the NFL Most Valuable Player Award in 1997 (with [[Brett Favre]]) after rushing for 2,053 yards in 16 games, becoming the third running back to surpass 2,000 yards. In the same season, Sanders totaled a record 2,358 yards from scrimmage, later surpassed by both [[Marshall Faulk]] and [[Chris Johnson (running back)|Chris Johnson]]. By the end of his career, Sanders was known as "one of the game's most electrifying runners", as described by the Pro Football Hall of Fame; this was a view shared by ''[[Sports Illustrated]],'' who described him as "running circles around NFL defenses with an electrifying style unlike anything the league has seen."<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Zimmerman |first=Paul |date=December 8, 1997 |title=Lion King Barry Sanders Is Running Circles Around NFL Defenses With An Electrifying Style Unlike Anything The League Has Seen |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1997/12/08/lion-king-barry-sanders-is-running-circles-around-nfl-defenses-with-an-electrifying-style-unlike-anything-the-league-has-seen |access-date=June 9, 2022 |magazine=[[Sports Illustrated]] |language=en-us}}</ref><ref name=":16" /> His 1989 season is regarded as one of the best all-time by a rookie running back, ranked No. 3 by NFL analyst Elliot Harrison, and No 4. by [[ESPN]] analyst Jeff Merron.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Harrison |first=Elliot |date=April 29, 2015 |title=Top rookie seasons of the Super Bowl era: Running backs |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/top-rookie-seasons-of-the-super-bowl-era-running-backs-0ap3000000488801 |access-date=June 9, 2022 |website=www.nfl.com |publisher=[[National Football League]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="ESPN best rookies">{{cite news |last=Merron |first=Jeff |date=September 2003 |title=LT best NFL rookie of all time |work=[[ESPN]] |url=https://www.espn.com/page2/s/list/nflrookies.html |url-status=live |access-date=August 12, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070816144913/http://espn.go.com/page2/s/list/nflrookies.html |archive-date=August 16, 2007}}</ref> In 1999, an ESPN survey of journalists, athletes, and other sports figures ranked Sanders as the 76th greatest North American athlete of the 20th century.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ESPN.com: Top N. American athletes of the century |url=https://www.espn.com/sportscentury/athletes.html |access-date=June 9, 2022 |website=www.espn.com |publisher=[[ESPN]]}}</ref>

Although he sat behind fellow Pro Football Hall of Fame running back Thurman Thomas on the [[depth chart]] for his first two collegiate seasons, Sanders is considered one of the greatest college football players of all time. His Heisman trophy-winning season in 1988, in which he set single-season college football records for most rushing yards gained, touchdowns scored, and total scrimmage yards (among other records), is often considered the greatest individual college football season ever, ranked No. 1 by ESPN and Sporting News.<ref name="ESPN Page2">{{cite news |last=Merron |first=Jeff |date=December 15, 2003 |title=Best individual college football seasons |url=https://www.espn.com/page2/s/list/collegefootball/seasons.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160924190445/https://www.espn.com/page2/s/list/collegefootball/seasons.html |archive-date=September 24, 2016 |access-date=July 14, 2017 |work=ESPN |quote=The only serious question when composing this list was 'Who's No. 2?'}}</ref><ref name=":15" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Iyer |first=Vinnie |date=January 14, 2020 |title=CFB 150: Top 10 individual single-season performances in college football history |url=https://www.sportingnews.com/us/ncaa-football/news/top-10-individual-single-season-performances-in-college-football-history/1s4bv13g9pu8o1r7j5hztadnik |access-date=June 9, 2022 |website=[[Sporting News]] |language=en}}</ref> In commemoration of the 150th year of college football, Sanders was honored during [[Half-time|halftime]] at the [[College Football Playoff National Championship]] game on January 13, 2020, as the No. 9 player of all time.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nagel |first=Cody |date=January 14, 2020 |title=Barry Sanders included among ESPN's Top 150 players |url=https://247sports.com/college/oklahoma-state/Article/Oklahoma-State-Barry-Sanders-ESPN-top-150-players-142163986/ |access-date=January 14, 2020 |website=GoPokes |publisher=[[247Sports]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

In contrast to many of the star players of his era, Sanders was noted for his on-field humility.{{Sfn|Crompton|2008|p=93}} Despite his flashy playing style, Sanders was rarely seen celebrating after the whistle was blown; instead, he handed the ball to a referee, and was never tempted into celebrating any further.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hruby |first=Patrick |title=Burning questions: Barry Sanders |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/page2/story?page=hruby/061120&src=mobile |access-date=June 15, 2022 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}}</ref> He was recognized for putting his team's success over his stats, as shown when he denied a request from head coach Wayne Fontes to return to play in a game so that he could gain enough rushing yards to become the rushing leader for that season.<ref name=":12" /> He disliked speaking to the press, and rarely spoke about his accomplishments publicly.<ref name=":23" /> When reflecting on his career, ESPN described Sanders as a "humble superstar."<ref name="JakeTrotter" />

==Personal life==
[[File:Barry J. Sanders (16493479564).jpg|thumb|Sanders' eldest son, [[Barry J. Sanders|Barry]], playing for the [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford Cardinal]]]]
Sanders is a Christian.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Barry Sanders Christian Faith {{!}} Detroit Lions |url=https://faithonthefieldshow.com/barry-sanders-christian-faith/ |access-date=June 8, 2022 |website=Faith on the Field |language=en-US}}</ref> He and his wife, Lauren Campbell Sanders, a former news anchor for [[WDIV]] in Detroit, filed for divorce in February 2012 after 12 years of marriage.<ref name=":26">{{Cite web |last=Zaldivar |first=Gabe |date=February 27, 2012 |title=Barry Sanders Divorce: NFL Legend and Lauren Campbell Reportedly Splitting |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1083149-barry-sanders-divorce-nfl-legend-and-lauren-campbell-reportedly-splitting |access-date=February 3, 2023 |website=[[Bleacher Report]] |language=en}}</ref> Sanders' brother, Byron, was the starting running back at [[Northwestern Wildcats football|Northwestern University]], and would be selected by the Chicago Bears in the 9th round of the [[1989 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1989 NFL draft |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1989/draft.htm |access-date=January 6, 2025 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Byron was cut by the Bears two months after joining the franchise.{{Sfn|Crompton|2008|p=29}}

Sanders has four sons: [[Barry J. Sanders]], Nick, Nigel, and Noah; the youngest three are from his marriage to Campbell.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bennett |first=Chuck |title=In Residence: Lauren Sanders - Detroit Home - Winter 2010 - Detroit, MI |url=http://www.detroithomemag.com/Detroit-Home/Winter-2010/In-Residence-Lauren-Sanders/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110318080049/http://www.detroithomemag.com/Detroit-Home/Winter-2010/In-Residence-Lauren-Sanders/ |archive-date=March 18, 2011 |access-date=January 15, 2014 |work=Detroit Home Magazine}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Barry Sanders |url=https://www.barrysanders.com/about.html |access-date=January 28, 2023 |website=www.barrysanders.com}}</ref> When the couple divorced, Sanders requested joint custody of them, while Campbell kept their medical coverage.<ref name=":26" /> Sanders' oldest son, Barry J. Sanders, played running back at [[Stanford University]] from 2012 to 2015, and Oklahoma State University in 2016.<ref name="espn.go.com">{{Cite news |last=Sayles |first=Damon |date=January 7, 2012 |title=Barry J. Sanders commits to Stanford |url=https://www.espn.com/college-sports/recruiting/football/story/_/id/7436402/espu-150-barry-j-sanders-commits-stanford-cardinal |access-date=January 15, 2014 |work=ESPN.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Trotter |first=Jake |author-link=Jake Trotter |date=February 11, 2016 |title=Barry J. Sanders to transfer to Oklahoma State, can play in '16 |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/14761502/barry-sanders-son-barry-j-sanders-plans-transfer-oklahoma-state-cowboys |access-date=June 6, 2024 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref> From 2022−2026, his son Nick played basketball at Michigan State University. In 2003, Sanders co-wrote his autobiography, ''Barry Sanders: Now You See Him: His Story In His Own Words,'' with Mark McCormick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Barry Sanders Now You See Him: His Story in His Own Words |url=https://www.allbookstores.com/Barry-Sanders-Now-You-See/9781578601394 |access-date=June 11, 2022 |website=www.allbookstores.com |language=en}}</ref> He has reportedly donated to several charities, under the condition that they do not disclose his participation in any of them.<ref name=":21" />

Sanders introduced ESPN's ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' game between the [[Chicago Bears]] and the Lions on October 10, 2011.<ref>{{cite news |date=October 8, 2011 |title=Barry Sanders to open MNF sans song |work=[[United Press International|UPI]] |url=http://www.upi.com/Sports_News/2011/10/08/Barry-Sanders-to-open-MNF-sans-song/UPI-86401318083352/ |access-date=October 8, 2011}}</ref> In April 2013, Sanders made it to the finals of the vote to be on the cover of [[EA Sports]] ''[[Madden NFL 25 (2013 video game)|Madden NFL 25]]'', which celebrated the game's 25th anniversary, by beating head coach [[Ron Rivera]] in Round One, running back [[Marcus Allen]] in Round Two, linebacker [[Ray Lewis]] in Round Three, quarterback [[Joe Montana]] in the quarter-finals, and wide receiver [[Jerry Rice]] in the semi-finals. In the final round, he defeated running back [[Adrian Peterson]] to become the next cover athlete, the first player to appear on the cover of ''[[Madden NFL|Madden NFL Football]]'' more than once (he appeared in the background of the ''[[Madden NFL 2000]]'' cover).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vote for EA Sports' 'Madden NFL 25' Cover Athlete - SportsNation #MaddenCoverVote - ESPN |url=http://espn.go.com/sportsnation/feature/madden25cover |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130517033035/http://espn.go.com/sportsnation/feature/madden25cover |archive-date=May 17, 2013 |access-date=January 15, 2014 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}}</ref><ref name="ESPN cover choice">{{Cite web |date=April 25, 2013 |title=Barry Sanders wins Madden vote |url=https://www.espn.com/sportsnation/story/_/id/9208257/barry-sanders-wins-madden-25-cover-vote-adrian-peterson-minnesota-vikings |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130604234350/http://espn.go.com/sportsnation/story/_/id/9208257/barry-sanders-wins-madden-25-cover-vote-adrian-peterson-minnesota-vikings |archive-date=June 4, 2013 |access-date=June 10, 2013 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}}</ref>

In December 2024, Sanders opened a new car wash in [[Madison Heights, Michigan]].<ref name="i463">{{cite web | title=Barry Sanders opens new car wash in Madison Heights | website=WXYZ 7 News Detroit | date=December 21, 2024 | url=https://www.wxyz.com/sports/barry-sanders-opens-new-car-wash-in-madison-heights | access-date=January 6, 2025}}</ref> On [[Father's Day]] weekend in 2025, he announced that he had suffered a heart attack the previous summer, and had a three-day hospital stay before being released after treatment. This led him to begin production of a documentary to educate the symptoms of [[cardiac arrest]], especially for former athletes more tempered to ignore instances of pain, like himself.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pouncey |first=Colton |date=June 13, 2025 |title=Lions Legend Barry Sanders Opens Up About Heart Attack, Hopes to Educate in New Documentary |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/6423192/2025/06/13/lions-barry-sanders-heart-attack-documentary/ |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[The Athletic]] |publisher=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

Quality control administrator | highlights = * Third-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] ([[2004 College Football All-America Team|2004]]) * First-team [[List of All-Big 12 Conference football teams|All-Big 12]] ([[2004 All-Big 12 Conference football team|2004]]) | statlabel1 = [[Tackle (football move)|Total tackles]] | statvalue1 = 657 | statlabel2 = [[Quarterback sack|Sacks]] | statvalue2 = 6.0 | statlabel3 = [[Fumble|Forced fumbles]] | statvalue3 = 7 | statlabel4 = [[Fumble|Fumble recoveries]] | statvalue4 = 5 | statlabel5 = [[Interceptions]] | statvalue5 = 7 | pfr = RuudBa20 }} '''Barrett James Ruud''' (born May 20, 1983) is an American [[American football|football]] coach who serves as inside linebackers coach for the [[Atlanta Falcons]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the second round of the [[2005 NFL draft]] and also played for the [[Tennessee Titans]], [[New Orleans Saints]], and [[Houston Texans]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska Cornhuskers]], where he was the inside linebackers coach from 2018 to 2022. ==Early life== Ruud attended high school at [[Lincoln Southeast High School]] in [[Lincoln, Nebraska]]. He was a four-year [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] and a two-time all-state honorable mention selection in basketball. He helped his team compile a 48–2 record and Class A state titles in 1998, 1999, and 2001. He was a two-time All-American by the [[Omaha World-Herald]] and earned [[All-American]] honors as a linebacker from Prep Star and Student Sport. Ruud also played halfback and set school career records with 2,988 rushing yards and 54 touchdowns. He also was a two-time super-state pick and was named offensive player of the year, defensive player of the year and prep athlete of the year by the ''[[Lincoln Journal Star]]''. Ruud's great-grandfather [[Clarence Swanson]] played college football for Nebraska from 1918 to 1921 and is an inductee of the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].{{cite news |url=https://www.ketv.com/article/huskers-throwback-thursday-bo-and-barrett-ruud/7648016 |title=Huskers Throwback Thursday: Bo and Barrett Ruud |website=[[KETV]] |date=September 4, 2014 |accessdate=May 14, 2024}} ==College career== Ruud played [[college football]] at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] becoming a third-generation Husker football player in the process. He earned numerous honors while there including 2004 Third-team All American, 2004 First-team All-[[Big 12]], 2003 Second-team All-Big 12, and 2002 All-Big 12 honorable mention among others. He finished his career starting 37 of 50 games finishing with a school record 432 career [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]]. ==Professional career== {{NFL predraft | height ft = 6 | height in = 2 1/2 | weight = 241 | dash = 4.78 | ten split = 1.68 | twenty split = 2.78 | shuttle = 3.94 | cone drill = 7.22 | vertical = 34.5 | broad ft = 9 | broad in = 4 | bench = 25 | arm span = 30 5/8 | hand span = 9 1/4 | note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]{{Cite web |url=https://draftscout.com/dsprofile.php?PlayerId=54896&DraftYear=2005 |title=Barrett Ruud College Football Profile |website=DraftScout.com |access-date=June 3, 2026}}{{Cite web |url=https://nflcombineresults.com/playerpage.php?f=Barrett&l=Ruud&i=7247 |title=Barrett Ruud Combine Results |website=NFLCombineResults.com |access-date=June 3, 2026}} }} ===Tampa Bay Buccaneers=== Ruud was selected by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in the second round of the [[2005 NFL draft]].{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=May 7, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} As a rookie, he played in all 16 games recording 17 tackles. In 2006, he started 5 of 16 games after injuries to [[Shelton Quarles]] and [[Ryan Nece]] and finished with 57 tackles. In 2007 Ruud became a full-time starter after the team cut longtime starter Quarles. He finished the season starting all 15 games he played in, recording 114 tackles and two [[interceptions]]. He remained the Buccaneers starter through 2008 and ended the season totaling 137 tackles, three sacks and two interceptions. ===Tennessee Titans=== On July 30, 2011, Ruud signed with the [[Tennessee Titans]]. On December 13, 2011, Ruud was placed on [[injured reserve]], ending his season.{{Cite web |date=2011-12-13 |title=Titans put Ruud on season-ending IR, ink Malast |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/7349775/tennessee-titans-put-barrett-ruud-season-ending-ir-sign-kevin-malast |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}} ===Seattle Seahawks=== In April 2012, Ruud signed with the [[Seattle Seahawks]].{{cite web | agency=Associated Press | title=NFL roundup: Seattle Seahawks sign Barrett Ruud, Roy Lewis and Deuce Lutui | website=Deseret News | date=2012-04-07 | url=https://www.deseret.com/2012/4/7/20405376/nfl-roundup-seattle-seahawks-sign-barrett-ruud-roy-lewis-and-deuce-lutui/ | access-date=2024-12-24}} ===New Orleans Saints=== On August 20, 2012, Ruud was traded to the [[New Orleans Saints]] in exchange for a conditional draft pick.{{Cite web |date=2012-08-21 |title=Saints acquire Seahawks LB Ruud for draft pick |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/trainingcamp12/story/_/id/8287394/new-orleans-saints-acquire-barrett-ruud-seattle-seahawks-draft-pick |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}} On October 8, 2012, Ruud was cut by the Saints after the team went through a 1–4 start. ===Houston Texans=== On October 10, 2012, Ruud was signed by the [[Houston Texans]], to provide depth at linebacker after the injury to defensive star [[Brian Cushing]].{{cite web | title=Texans sign Barrett Ruud, release Trindon Holliday | website=Houston Texans | date=2012-10-10 | url=https://www.houstontexans.com/news/texans-sign-barrett-ruud-release-trindon-holliday-8522381 | access-date=2025-01-06}} ===NFL statistics=== {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- ! rowspan="2"| Year ! rowspan="2"| Team ! rowspan="2"| GP ! colspan="4"| Tackles ! colspan="2"| Fumbles ! colspan="6"| Interceptions |- ! '''Barry Foster''' (born December 8, 1968) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arkansas Razorbacks football|Arkansas Razorbacks]].

==Summary==
Foster attended [[Duncanville High School]] in Texas. He went on to attend the [[University of Arkansas]], where he played fullback for the [[Arkansas Razorbacks|Razorbacks]] alongside a pair of tailbacks, [[James Rouse (American football)|James Rouse]] and E. D. Jackson, in [[Ken Hatfield]]'s [[Wishbone formation|wishbone offense]]. Foster wore #18 for his entire time at Arkansas (1987–1989). Foster helped the Razorbacks win back-to-back [[Southwest Conference]] championships in 1988 and 1989, making consecutive trips to the [[Cotton Bowl Classic]] in Dallas on New Year's Day. The Razorbacks finished each of these seasons with a 10–2 record, and were ranked in the final polls' top 15. After only three collegiate seasons, he decided to forgo his senior year after Hatfield left to coach Clemson, and entered the 1990 NFL Draft. He was selected by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] with the 19th pick of the fifth round (128th overall) by [[Chuck Noll]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1990 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1990/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-25 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Foster was 5'10", weighed 223 lbs, and wore #29 for the Steelers.

Barry Foster's NFL career was cut short because of injuries. For his career, he carried the football 915 times for 3,943 yards, a 4.3-yard per carry average, caught 93 passes for 804 receiving yards, scored 28 touchdowns, and went to 2 Pro Bowls. His 1,690 rushing yards in 1992 remain a Steelers single-season rushing record. Foster was known in the 90's as "The NFL's Other Barry.", a reference to himself and [[Barry Sanders]].

==Playing career==

In 1990, Foster was used primarily on special teams during his rookie season. It was during this first season that he made a catastrophic blunder in a game that Steelers played against the 49ers on October 21. He was positioned to receive a kick-off, but did not field the kick because he thought that the ball would be downed by the coverage team, not realizing that the dead ball rule only applies to punts and that the kick was a de facto fumble when he didn't secure it. The result was a San Francisco recovery that eventually lead to a Steelers loss. This is one of the handful of times in NFL history that a player neglected to field a kick-off on the return team.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/10/22/sports/nfl-blunder-by-a-steeler-helps-49ers-go-to-6-0.html|title=N.F.L.; Blunder by a Steeler Helps 49ers Go to 6-0|newspaper=The New York Times|date=October 22, 1990}}</ref>
 
His second NFL season, in 1991, started out with a 121-yard rushing game with a 56-yard touchdown run against the [[Buffalo Bills]] in week 2 but he sprained his ankle a few weeks later and missed five games.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Barry Foster 1991 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FostBa00/gamelog/1991/ |access-date=2025-07-13 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

In 1992, Barry Foster got the [[Bill Cowher]] era going in Pittsburgh after two seasons on the bench backing up former first-round pick [[Tim Worley]]. After Worley was suspended the entire year from the NFL due to missing two mandatory drug tests,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=860&dat=19920430&id=gjgQAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Uo8DAAAAIBAJ&pg=4266,6151151|title=Ellensburg Daily Record - Google News Archive Search}}</ref> Foster got the starting nod and rushed for a Steelers single season record 1,690 yards and also broke [[Franco Harris]]'s team record for 100-yard games in a season with 12, that also tied [[Eric Dickerson]]'s [[NFL]] record for 100-yard games. He was voted to the [[Pro Bowl]] that year and also scored 11 touchdowns. Foster finished 1992 as the AFC's top rusher and second to Emmitt Smith by 23 yards for the rushing title. Foster's strong season, combined with the struggling Worley being traded to the [[Chicago Bears]] after the season, led to Foster being the unquestioned starter moving forward.

In 1993, Foster's season started off strong, but injuries limited him to 711 yards in nine games with eight touchdowns. Despite the injuries, Foster still made the Pro Bowl for the second year in a row.

In 1994, Foster played 11 games (again limited due to injuries) and gained 851 yards. During a September 18, 1994 game against the [[Indianapolis Colts]], he rushed for 179 yards on 31 carries and a touchdown. He added three catches for another 13 yards – giving him more yards than the entire Colts’ offense. The game was billed as Barry Foster versus [[Marshall Faulk]], but it was no contest. “He (Faulk) wasn't the challenge,” said Foster. “I respond to the challenge the defense gives me". The injury to Foster that year opened the door for rookie running back [[Bam Morris]] to take over.

The 1994 AFC Championship game would not only be Foster's last game in a Steeler uniform, but his last NFL game. Trailing the [[San Diego Chargers]] 17–13, the Steelers were mounting the go-ahead drive. On the last play of the game, a fourth down and goal from the three-yard line, Foster was in primarily as a blocker for Neil O'Donnell, but when San Diego sent no pass rush, Foster ran out of the backfield to become an eligible receiver on a short underneath route. The throw from O'Donnell was delayed and gave San Diego linebacker [[Dennis Gibson (American football)|Dennis Gibson]] the chance to reach over Foster and bat the ball to the ground as Foster was falling to the turf of Three Rivers stadium. That play ended the Steelers' season. O'Donnell later stated that Foster was his fourth read on that play.

In 1995, Barry Foster had become expendable due to his contract, the rise of Bam Morris, the signing of former 1,000-yard running back [[Erric Pegram]], injuries, and (more long-term) the [[Jerome Bettis trade|forthcoming trade]] for future [[Pro Football Hall of Fame|Hall of Famer]] [[Jerome Bettis]] the following year. Pittsburgh traded Foster to the expansion [[Carolina Panthers]], but he was cut in training camp when he failed a physical, after which he retired.

Later that season, Foster came out of retirement to sign with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] after the injury to their first-round draft pick [[Ki-Jana Carter]] in the preseason. But two days after signing a $1 million contract, Foster changed his mind and left the Bengals. Foster, age 26, out of football since the Carolina Panthers released him before the 1995 season began, complained that he felt like "a 60-year-old running back" after his first workout in pads with the team. He later returned his reported $300,000 signing bonus to the Bengals, left town, and retired again a few days later without playing a game. He announced that he had saved his money and had enough to retire.

==Since Retirement==

After Foster retired from the NFL, he became the running backs coach at DeLay Middle School, and went on to be an Assistant Principal at Crosswinds Accelerated High School in Grand Prairie, Texas. Currently, he is an assistant Principal at Hillwood Middle School in Fort Worth, TX.

'''Byron''' "'''Bam"''' '''Morris''' (born January 13, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], [[Chicago Bears]], [[Baltimore Ravens]], and the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

==Early life==
Morris attended [[Texas Tech University]] where he won the 1993 [[Doak Walker Award]] as the top running back in [[college football]]. Among other accomplishments while playing for the [[Texas Tech Red Raiders|Red Raiders]], Morris was ranked second in the nation in rushing yards per game in 1993.<ref name="Morris">{{cite news |url=http://media.www.dailytoreador.com/media/storage/paper870/news/2007/04/02/Sports/Vote-In.Our.Poll.Byron.Morris.And.Byron.Hanspard-2816050.shtml?reffeature=htmlemailedition |title=Vote in our poll: Byron Morris and Byron Hanspard |newspaper=[[The Daily Toreador]] |date=April 2, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929084021/http://media.www.dailytoreador.com/media/storage/paper870/news/2007/04/02/Sports/Vote-In.Our.Poll.Byron.Morris.And.Byron.Hanspard-2816050.shtml?reffeature=htmlemailedition |archive-date=September 29, 2007 }}</ref> He was selected by the Pittsburgh Steelers with the 91st overall pick in the [[1994 NFL draft]] (3rd round). His older brother [[Ron Morris (American football)|Ron Morris]] played for the [[Chicago Bears]] and collegiately at [[Southern Methodist University]] (SMU). Their older brother J.C. Morris played college football at [[Texas Christian University]] (TCU).<ref>{{cite web|title=Passing the Bucks|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8i0EAAAAMBAJ&q=jc+morris+cooper+tx&pg=PA226|work=Texas Monthly|date = September 1983}}</ref>

==Professional career==
Morris was selected by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the third round of the [[1994 NFL draft]] with the 91st overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1994 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1994/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> During his NFL career, he recorded 3,809 yards on 974 attempts and scored 35 [[touchdown]]s during 75 games. He also caught 103 passes for 790 yards and one touchdown. He was the leading rusher for the Steelers in their [[Super Bowl XXX]] loss to the Cowboys, gaining 73 yards on 19 carries and a touchdown.

==Off-field issues==
Morris has become more well known for his off-field legal troubles than his football prowess. On June 27, 1996, Morris pleaded guilty to [[felony]] possession of [[marijuana]] in a [[plea bargain]] deal in front of a [[Rockwall County, Texas]], judge. Police testified that they found 6 pounds of marijuana during a traffic stop. He was fined $7,000 and sentenced to 200 hours of community service and six years' probation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bradford |first=Chris |title=Tough to a fault: Bam Morris' wild story 20 years after Super Bowl XXX |url=https://www.timesonline.com/story/sports/nfl/2016/02/06/tough-to-fault-bam-morris/18574778007/ |access-date=2021-01-29 |work=The Times}}</ref>

He was cut by the Steelers after the guilty plea and signed as a [[free agent]] with the Baltimore Ravens. After two seasons, both marked with suspensions concerning the NFL's substance abuse policy, Morris was released. He signed with the Chicago Bears the following year, but was cut after playing in only two regular season games. He then signed with the Kansas City Chiefs.

Morris pleaded guilty in August 2001 to two counts of federal [[Illegal drug trade|drug trafficking]] and was sentenced to 30 months in prison. As part of the plea bargain, Morris admitted to distributing more than 100 kilograms of marijuana in the Kansas City area between 1998 and 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/bam-morris-pleads-guilty/|title=Bam Morris Pleads Guilty|website=[[CBS News]]|date=August 14, 2000 }}</ref>

On September 10, 2001, Morris was convicted of violating his parole stemming from his 1996 plea bargain and sentenced to 10 years in a Texas prison. He was released early on February 29, 2004.

He played [[arena football]] with the Katy Copperheads in 2006.

'''Barry Sims''' (born December 1, 1974) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive lineman]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Utah Utes football|Utah Utes]] and was selected by the [[Scottish Claymores]] in the 17th round of the [[NFL Europa|NFL Europe Draft]] in 1999. Sims played nine seasons in the NFL with the [[Oakland Raiders]] and three seasons with the [[San Francisco 49ers]].

==Early life==
Sims lettered in football, basketball and track at [[Park City High School]] (Utah).  He was all-League as a two-way lineman.  In basketball, Sims played forward and center as well as participated in track as a shot putter, high jumper, and long jumper.  On October 15, 2009, Sims' #72 Park City Miners football jersey was the first ever to be retired at that school.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.topix.net/forum/sports/T15N9RTT7FD7RQ9TF | title=Quizzes | Free Online Quizzes | PCHquizzes | access-date=August 25, 2010 | archive-date=October 15, 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121015134728/http://www.topix.net/forum/sports/T15N9RTT7FD7RQ9TF | url-status=dead }}</ref>

==College career==
Sims played two years at the [[University of Utah]] after transferring there from [[Dixie Junior College]] where he was named "Most Improved Player."  He earned a BS in sociology from the University of Utah and finished with All-[[Western Athletic Conference|WAC]] honors.

==Professional career==
Sims has, {{As of|2010|lc=on}}, played in 152 NFL games with 133 starts, seven playoff starts, two Conference Championships and one Super Bowl appearance.

===Scottish Claymores===
Sims was drafted in the 17th round of the [[NFL Europa|NFL European League]] draft by the [[Scottish Claymores]].  He played there in the spring of 1999. Sims was inducted into the Scottish Claymores Hall of Fame in 2004.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.claymores.co.uk/team/hof/index.php |title=Scottish Claymores: Hall of Fame |accessdate=August 19, 2008 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080510151829/http://www.claymores.co.uk/team/hof/index.php |archivedate=May 10, 2008 }}</ref>

===Oakland Raiders===
The [[Oakland Raiders]] picked Sims up as a free agent during training camp in 1999.  He broke into the starting lineup at left tackle in his fifth game facing off against All-Pro [[Bruce Smith (defensive end)|Bruce Smith]].  He started the entire 2004 season at left tackle and was co-recipient of the 2004 Commitment to Excellence Award which exemplifies the Pride and Spirit of the [[Oakland Raiders]].  During the 2005 season, Sims was the only member of the offensive line to play every snap from scrimmage through 16 league games.  During the 2006 season, Sims moved inside to left guard.  He was injured during his seventh game and sidelined for the rest of the season, thereby snapping a 67-game consecutive start streak.  During the 2007 season, Sims competed with top draft pick [[Robert Gallery]] to regain his position as the starter at left tackle. He was also named a team captain during that season as the longest tenured starter on the team.  On February 29, 2008, Sims was subsequently released by the Raiders to meet upcoming salary cap requirements.

===San Francisco 49ers===
Sims was signed by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] on June 23, 2008, primarily as a veteran back-up tackle. However, Sims has been called on to start at both left and right tackle positions, with eight starts at left tackle during the 2009 season, ably filling in for regular starter [[Joe Staley]]. Following the 2010 season, Sims was not re-signed by the 49ers.

==Personal life==
Barry is an avid golfer who also enjoys hiking, cycling, and skiing.  Sims lives with his wife Shae in  Park City, Utah. They are very active in a variety of charitable activities, including Foster a Dream, which supports [[Northern California]] foster youth and [[Special Olympics]] of Northern California.

'''Barrett Nicholas Green''' (born October 29, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia Mountaineers]] and was selected in the second round (50th overall) by the [[Detroit Lions]] in the [[2000 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2000 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2000/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life==
Green was born in [[West Palm Beach, Florida]] and attended [[Suncoast High School]]. At Suncoast, he was a wrestler and played baseball along with football. Following his senior season he played in the South Florida All-Star Game.<ref name="Lions">{{cite web|url=http://www.detroitlions.com/bio.cfm?bio_id=34 |title=#54 Barrett Green |work=[[Detroit Lions]] |accessdate=2009-08-21 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20060317152532/http://www.detroitlions.com/bio.cfm?bio_id=34 |archivedate=March 17, 2006 }}</ref>

==College career==
As a true freshman in 1995, Green [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirted]] but was still named Rookie of the Year due to his performance on the [[scout team]]. In 1996, Green was the back up [[strong safety]] and played in every game. For the season he recorded 12 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]] and a pass deflection. Green was elevated to the starting strong safety as a redshirt sophomore in 1997 and played in every game. He finished third on West Virginia with 71 tackles and also had three [[Quarterback sack|sacks]]. Green added a fumble recovery, six pass deflections and four [[interceptions]] to his season totals. Against [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]] he had nine tackles which was his season high and he also had eight tackles against [[Maryland Terrapins football|Maryland]]. Green recorded the longest non-touchdown interception return in [[Mountaineer Field]] history with an 83-yard return against [[Rutgers Scarlet Knights football|Rutgers]]. In 1998, Green moved forward to the starting [[Linebacker#Weakside linebacker|weak-side linebacker]] and added 84 more tackles than the previous season with a team–leading 155 tackles and set a school record with 107 solo tackles. His 155 tackles was the seventh best in West Virginia school history. His season high in tackles was 19 against [[Navy Midshipmen football|Navy]] and [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami (Fla.)]]. He added 15 tackles against [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse]] and 14 in the [[Boston College Eagles football|Boston College]] game. In the [[1998 Insight.com Bowl]] against [[Missouri Tigers football|Missouri]], he played with a cracked rib and yet he still recorded a team high 14 tackles. Following the season he was named First team All Big East. Green was named First team All Big East for a second straight year in 1999 a season in which he led the team once again with 126 tackles. Three sacks and seven tackles for a loss added to his season totals. He recorded 18 tackles against Navy, 17 against [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech]] and 15 against Syracuse.<ref name="Lions" />

'''Barret Glenn Robbins''' (August 26, 1973 – March 26, 2026) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[center (gridiron football)|center]] for nine seasons with the [[Oakland Raiders]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). After playing [[college football]] for the [[TCU Horned Frogs football|TCU Horned Frogs]], he was taken by the Raiders in the second round of the [[1995 NFL draft]]. He was elected to the [[Pro Bowl]] in 2002.

==College career==
Robbins attended [[Texas Christian University]], where he played for the [[TCU Horned Frogs football|Horned Frogs]]. As a [[senior (education)|senior]] in [[1994 TCU Horned Frogs football team|1994]], he was named first-team [[List of All-Southwest Conference football teams|All-Southwest Conference]]. TCU played in the [[1994 Independence Bowl]], their first postseason game in a decade.<ref>{{cite news|first=Mac|last=Engel|title=Former TCU great and troubled Raiders Pro Bowler Barret Robbins has died|date=March 27, 2026|newspaper=Fort Worth Star-Telegram|url=https://www.star-telegram.com/sports/spt-columns-blogs/mac-engel/article315209614.html|access-date=March 28, 2026}}</ref> While in college, Robbins was diagnosed with [[Major depressive disorder|depression]] and [[Generalized anxiety disorder|anxiety]], and he was hospitalized during a [[psychotic episode]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Matt|last=Moret|title=Former All-Pro Raiders center Barret Robbins dead at 52|date=March 27, 2026|work=The Athletic|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7152530/2026/03/27/barret-robbins-raiders-obituary/|url-access=subscription|access-date=March 28, 2026}}</ref>

==Professional career==

Robbins was selected by the Los Angeles Raiders in the second round of the [[1995 NFL draft]], with the 49th overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1995 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1995/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

In 1996, [[Mike White (American football coach)|Mike White]]'s last year as head coach, the second-year Robbins replaced [[Dan Turk]] in the lineup, becoming only the fifth starting center in Raider history, after Turk, [[Don Mosebar]], [[Dave Dalby]], and [[Jim Otto]]. The first sign of his mental health problems turned up during the season when he was found disoriented and wandering around the team hotel in Denver shortly before a game with the [[Denver Broncos]]. Robbins missed that game and was hospitalized.<ref name=si>{{cite web |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/2015/12/16/untold-super-bowl-barret-robbins-raiders |title = When Raiders' Barret Robbins disappeared before Super Bowl XXXVII - Sports Illustrated| date=15 December 2015 }}</ref>

During the [[2000 NFL season]] with [[Jon Gruden]] as head coach and [[Rich Gannon]] at quarterback, Oakland scored 479 points (29.9 points/game), 3rd of 31 teams in the NFL, thanks to a strong offensive line which included Robbins playing between [[Steve Wisniewski]] at left guard and [[Mo Collins (American football)|Mo Collins]] at right guard in all 16 games (also both playoff games), finishing with a won-lost record of 12–4 and an [[AFC West]] title. In the divisional round of the [[2000–01 NFL playoffs]], Oakland shut out the [[Miami Dolphins]] 27–0, gaining 140 yards on the ground. An early sign of Robbins' future trouble was displayed when he went missing a week before the AFC championship game, though in this case he did show up 24 hours before the game started and played in the Raiders 16–3 loss to the [[Baltimore Ravens]].<ref name=si/>

During the [[2001 NFL season]], Robbins was injured, playing in only two regular season games, replaced by [[Adam Treu]] (also in both playoff games), when Oakland scored 399 points (24.9 points/game), 4th of 31 teams in the NFL, and won the AFC west again with a 10–6 record, defeating the [[New York Jets]] in a wildcard game but losing to the [[New England Patriots]] in the divisional round, in controversial fashion (see [[Tuck Rule Game]]).

In the [[2002 NFL season]] with [[Bill Callahan (American football coach)|Bill Callahan]] in his first year as head coach, Robbins rebounded strongly by starting all 16 regular season games and making the [[Pro Bowl]]. Oakland won the AFC west for the third straight year, with an 11–5 record, scoring 450 points (28.1 points/game), 2nd of 32 teams in the NFL. In the [[2002–03 NFL playoffs]], the Raiders defeated the [[New York Jets]] again with 399 total yards, with an offensive line composed of Robbins, [[Frank Middleton]] and [[Mo Collins (American football)|Mo Collins]] at guard, [[Barry Sims]] and [[Lincoln Kennedy]] at tackle. The Raiders then beat with the same offensive line the [[Tennessee Titans]] in the AFC championship game, gaining 375 total yards.

Then, the day before [[Super Bowl XXXVII]], Robbins was reported as missing for most of the day before the game after not taking his [[depression (mood)|depression]] medication. When he resurfaced that night, he was so incoherent that he didn't even know where he was.<ref name=WaPoDismiss>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/2003/01/30/raiders-callahan-robbins-was-incoherent/17cd1811-6d3b-4098-8de2-dde87b11b7cf|title=Raiders' Callahan: Robbins Was 'Incoherent'|author1=Steve Fainaru|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=January 30, 2003}}</ref> According to one of his teammates, Robbins didn't even recognize Callahan. Despite this, [[Al Davis]] still wanted Robbins in the game, and development coach [[Willie Brown (American football)|Willie Brown]] had Robbins running sprints in the parking lot on the morning of the game to see if he could still play.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Ultimate Super Bowl Book |last=McGinn |first=Bob |year=2009 |publisher=MVP Books |location=[[Minneapolis]] |isbn=978-0-7603-3651-9 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/ultimatesuperbow00mcgi_0 }}</ref>

Callahan had initially intended to let Robbins play, but not start. However, he ultimately decided to suspend Robbins for the game after concluding that he was not fit to take the field at all. He initially wanted to fly Robbins back to [[Oakland, California|Oakland]], but was unable to get him a plane ticket because he was missing his wallet and identification.<ref name=WaPoDismiss/> He spent 30 days at the [[Betty Ford Center]], during which time he was diagnosed with [[bipolar disorder]] (or manic-depressive disorder). He'd been diagnosed with depression while at TCU, but it is common for the two to be confused in the early stages. It turned out that he had gone into a manic episode after not taking his medication. According to his wife, Robbins spent most of the day before the Super Bowl partying across the border in [[Tijuana]], Mexico; he had thought the Raiders already won the game and he was celebrating their "victory."<ref name=Knapp>Knapp, Gwen. [https://www.sfgate.com/sports/article/6-years-later-Robbins-still-finding-his-way-3174246.php 6 years later, Robbins still finding his way]. [[San Francisco Chronicle]], 2009-01-31.</ref> With [[Adam Treu]] as the starting center, the Raiders were blown out in an ugly loss in the Super Bowl to the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], 48–21.

Robbins regained his starting job the next year in the [[2003 NFL season]] with the same linemates, a disastrous 4–12 for the team. However, his name and those of several of his teammates were found on the list of clients of the [[Bay Area Laboratory Co-operative]] that had given performance-enhancing drugs to [[Marion Jones]] and others. The Raiders released him in the summer of 2004 after he tested positive for "[[Tetrahydrogestrinone|the clear]]," a [[steroid]] known to have come from the BALCO lab.<ref name=Knapp/> Treu replaced him as the starting center.

==Post-football troubles==
A few months later, on Christmas Eve of 2004, Robbins was arrested for punching a security guard who tried to keep him from going to a bar at the [[Sir Francis Drake Hotel]] in San Francisco.<ref name=Knapp/> On January 15, 2005, Robbins was shot three times during a brawl with police in [[Miami Beach, Florida|Miami Beach]], and was subsequently charged with [[attempted murder]] for his role. Under a plea agreement, Robbins pleaded guilty to five charges, including the attempted murder charge, and was sentenced to five years' probation, ordered to receive treatment for his bipolar disorder, and to avoid alcohol. He spent years in jail or in rehab facilities due to problems with substance abuse. He ultimately ended up in a rehab facility in Houston in 2008, and was transferred to a halfway house in May 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=4256326 |website=ESPN.com |title=Robbins says he's looking to his future |date=June 13, 2009}}</ref>

In a 2009 interview with [[HBO]]'s [[Real Sports with Bryant Gumbel|''Real Sports'']], Robbins told [[Andrea Kremer]] that before being diagnosed as bipolar, he had dealt with his mood swings by taking alcohol, [[cocaine]], [[marijuana]], and steroids. He also said that he had been in a manic mood for both Raider playoff games prior to the Super Bowl. His ex-wife, Marisa, also interviewed for the story, said that before the diagnosis there were days where he had breakfast and went right back to bed.<ref>Gay, Nancy. [http://nfl.fanhouse.com/2009/07/20/barret-robbins-road-to-recovery-the-subject-of-hbos-real-spor Barret Robbins' Road to Recovery the Subject of HBO's 'Real Sports'] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110209192537/http://nfl.fanhouse.com/2009/07/20/barret-robbins-road-to-recovery-the-subject-of-hbos-real-spor |date=2011-02-09 }}. [[FanHouse]], 2009-07-30.</ref>

In early 2010, a police officer pulled him over near Dallas and found [[crack cocaine]] in his car.<ref>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/ex-nfl-lineman-robbins-gets-5-years-in-prison-for-drug-related-probation-violation/2011/03/25/AFcnPUXB_story.html Ex-NFL lineman Robbins gets 5 years in prison for drug-related probation violation]{{dead link|date=June 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> On March 25, 2011, Robbins was sentenced to five years in a Florida prison for a drug-related probation violation and was released on September 25, 2012.<ref>[https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2012/09/25/ex-raiders-center-barret-robbins-released-from-prison/ Ex-Raiders center Barret Robbins released from prison]</ref>

In August 2016, Robbins was alleged to have punched a mother and her daughter in [[Boca Raton, Florida]], resulting in his arrest and two subsequent charges of felony battery before being sent to a mental health facility.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Milian |first=Jorge |date=August 12, 2016 |title=Boca police: Former Oakland Raiders center punched women at hotel |url=http://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/news/crime-law/boca-police-former-oakland-raiders-center-punched-/nsD7w/ |newspaper=[[The Palm Beach Post]] |location=[[West Palm Beach, Florida]] |access-date=August 15, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Tasch |first=Justin |date=August 12, 2016 |title=Barret Robbins, who went MIA at Super Bowl, accused of randomly punching mother and daughter at Florida hotel |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/barret-robbins-accused-randomly-punching-women-hotel-article-1.2748573 |newspaper=[[New York Daily News]] |location=New York City |access-date=August 15, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Mano |first=Daniel |date=August 12, 2016 |title=Ex-Raider Barret Robbins charged with assaulting women in Florida |url=http://www.mercurynews.com/raiders/ci_30238018/barret-robbins-charged-assaulting-woman-and-her-daughter |newspaper=[[San Jose Mercury News]] |location=[[San Jose, California]] |access-date=August 15, 2016}}</ref>

In November 2020, Robbins was accused of leaving a restaurant in [[Delray Beach, Florida]], without paying for his meal.  A restaurant employee followed Robbins as he fled the restaurant on foot.  During the altercation, Robbins allegedly threw a rock at the restaurant employee. Delray Beach Police were called and Robbins was taken into custody.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://florida.arrests.org/Arrests/Barret_Robbins_46296850/ | title=Barret Robbins Mugshot | 11/14/20 Florida Arrest }}{{dead link|date=July 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite AV media| url-status = live| archive-url = https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211211/GpktyZ_dvsA| archive-date = 2021-12-11| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GpktyZ_dvsA| title = Former Oakland Raiders Star Barret Robbins Arrested in Delray Beach | website=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

==Death==
Robbins died on March 26, 2026, at the age of 52.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Byington |first1=Alex |title=Ex-Oakland Raiders All-Pro OL Barret Robbins dead at 52 |url=https://www.on3.com/pro/news/report-ex-oakland-raiders-all-pro-ol-barret-robbins-dead-at-52/ |access-date=27 March 2026 |publisher=On3 |date=27 March 2026}}</ref>

'''Barney Lewis Chavous''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|tʃ|eɪ|v|ʌ|s}} {{respell|CHAY|vuhs}};<ref>[https://media.denverbroncos.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/1977.pdf Denver Broncos 1977 Media Guide (pronunciations on page 141).] Retrieved June 8, 2020</ref> born March 22, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for the [[Denver Broncos]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for [[South Carolina State Bulldogs football|South Carolina State Bulldogs]]. He was selected by the [[Associated Press]] as a first-team defensive end on the [[1972 Little All-America college football team]].<ref name=":2">{{cite news|title=UC Davis QB Is Little All-American|newspaper=Santa Cruz Sentinel|date=December 6, 1972|page=22|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/89272815/uc-davis-qb-is-little-all-american/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> He was selected by the Broncos in the second round of the [[1973 NFL draft]]. He played 13 seasons with the Broncos, during which time the team had 11 winning seasons. At the time he retired, he was the Broncos all-time leader in quarterback sacks, and is fourth all-time (through 2025). He was part of the Broncos "[[Orange Crush Defense]]" that led the Broncos to [[Super Bowl XII]].

== Early life ==
Chavous was born on March 22, 1951, in [[Aiken, South Carolina]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Barney Chavous Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/C/ChavBa20.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> His family went back seven generations in Aiken, and he worked on his family farm as a child.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=Barney Chavous |url=https://www.coloradosports.org/hall-of-fame/athletes/2024-inductees/barney-chavous/ |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Colorado Sports Hall of Fame |language=en-US}}</ref> He graduated from Schofield High School in Aiken, where he started playing on the school's football team as a 6 ft 2 in (1.88 m) 210 lb (95.3 kg) junior.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |date=January 31, 1973 |title=Aikenite Drafted By Denver Broncos |work=Aiken Standard (Aiken, South Carolina) |pages=6–A |agency=Associated Press}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=December 1, 1972 |title=Local Player Accepts Shrine Bowl Invitation |work=Aiken Standard (Aiken, South Carolina) |pages=8}}</ref><ref name=":3" />

== College career ==
Chavous attended [[South Carolina State University]]. He started four years as a [[defensive end]] on the school's football team the [[South Carolina State Bulldogs football|Bulldogs]], playing under head coach [[Oree Banks]] in the  [[Mid-Eastern Athletic Conference]] (MEAC).<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Foster |first=Dan |date=September 8, 1972 |title=Orangeburg's Oree |work=The Greenville News (Greenville, South Carolina) |pages=26}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> It has also been reported that he played both defensive end and [[defensive tackle]] in college.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 2, 1971 |title=Bulldogs Can't Afford The Same Mistakes Today |work=The Times and Democrat (Orangeburg, South Carolina) |pages=8}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite news |date=February 3, 2008 |title=Ex-Bulldog Chavous: 'You cannot forget where we came from' |work=The Times and Democrat (Orangeburg, South Carolina) |pages=B6}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> 

The 6 ft 4 in (1.93 m) 250 lb (113.4 kg) Chavous was the Bulldogs' team captain as a senior in 1972. He was consistently timed at running the [[40-yard dash]] in 4.7 or 4.8 seconds. As a senior he averaged 10 unassisted [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]] per game, and was known for his quickness and mobility as a [[Pass rush|pass rusher]]. The [[Associated Press]] named Chavous a first-team [[Little All-America team|Little All-American]] at defensive end that year, and Chavous was also selected first-team All-MEAC.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite news|title=Barney Chavous Named Little All-America|date=December 6, 1972|pages=2B|work=The Times and Democrat (Orange, South Carolina)}}</ref><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":7" /> Overall he was named to eight different All-America teams in 1972.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|title=Schofield Grad To Play For Broncos|last=Hunter|first=Scott|date=July 12, 1973|pages=11|work=Aiken Standard (Aiken, South Carolina)}}</ref>  

In 1972, as a senior, he was the first South Carolina State player ever invited to play in the [[North–South Shrine Game|North-South Shrine Game]] in [[Miami]].<ref name=":0" /> He was also selected to play in the [[Senior Bowl]], as well as the [[Coaches All-America Game]] in [[Lubbock, Texas]].<ref name=":3" />

== Professional career ==
The [[Denver Broncos]] selected Chavous in the second round of the 1973 NFL draft, 36th overall.<ref>{{Cite web|title=1973 NFL Draft Listing|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1973/draft.htm|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com|access-date=2026-01-22|language=en}}</ref> He was surprised how high he was chosen, anticipating a possible selection in the fifth or sixth round; and was also surprised that Denver drafted him as he was not aware of their interest in him before then.<ref name=":1" /> He played his entire NFL career with the Broncos from 1973 to 1985, and was a key member of the Broncos' "[[Orange Crush Defense]]" of the 1970s.<ref name=":4" /> In 1973, he was reported to be 6 ft 4 in (1.93 m) 255 lb (115.7 kg) when he came to the Broncos' training camp.<ref name=":3" /> His NFL playing height and weight have also been listed as 6 ft 3 in 252 lb (114 kg).<ref name=":4" /> 

As a rookie in 1973 Chavous started all 14 Broncos games, with six [[Quarterback sack|quarterback sacks]] and two [[Fumble|fumble recoveries]].<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=1973 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1973.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> It was reported in late July 1973 the Broncos began using Chavous as their starting left defensive end in training camp;<ref>{{Cite news |date=July 29, 1973 |title=Rookie To Aid Denver Broncos |work=The Daily Sentinel (Grand Junction, Colorado) |pages=15}}</ref> and reported in August that he played left defensive end in 1973 preseason games, with [[Pete Duranko]] moved to tackle to make room for Chavous at end.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Caughman |first=Marv |date=August 23, 1973 |title=Chavous To Be Only Starting Rookie |work=The Times and Democrat (Orangeburg, South Carolina) |pages=2B}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Olderman |first=Murray |date=August 10, 1973 |title=Pro Charts, AFC West: Denver Broncos |work=The Waxahachie Daily Light (Waxahachie, Texas) |pages=4}}</ref> It was reported the following August that Chavous had started every Broncos' game in the 1973 season at defensive end.<ref name=":8">{{Cite news |last=McGee |first=Marty |date=August 4, 1974 |title=Football Misses Barney Chavous |work=Times and Democrat (Orangeburg, South Carolina) |pages=11A}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Broncos Tie Raiders 23–23|date=October 23, 1973|pages=12|work=Winston-Salem Journal (Winston-Salem, North Carolina)|agency=Associated Press}}</ref> Chavous was named the [[NFL Players Association|National Football League Players Association]] Rookie of the Year and ''[[Pittsburgh Courier]]'' Rookie of the Year, and  [[United Press International]] and ''[[Pro Football Weekly]]'' named him to their All-Rookie teams at defensive end.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite news|title=Ferguson On NFL All Rookie Team|last=Carnicelli|first=Joe|date=December 14, 1973|pages=5-B|work=The Longview Daily News (Longview, Texas)|agency=United Press International}}</ref><ref name=":8" /> It has also been stated that he was the Broncos starting right defensive tackle in the 1973 season.<ref name=":11" />

In 1974, he started 14 games at left defensive end and had a career-high nine sacks, and two fumble recoveries.<ref name=":4" /> Defensive coach [[Doc Urich|Doc Urick]] taught Chavous how to develop his pass rushing technique, rather than just relying on strength to manhandle offensive linemen; and to use film study on opposing linemen to prepare for games. In a November 1974 game against the [[1974 Baltimore Colts season|Baltimore Colts]], Chavous sacked Colts' quarterback [[Marty Domres]] four times. He also appeared to have an interception in that game, but was questionably ruled out of bounds by the officials. He received the Broncos' game ball for his defensive play in the game.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Snyder |first=Cameron C. |date=November 11, 1976 |title=Broncos top Colts, 17 to 6 |work=The Sun (Baltimore, Maryland) |pages=C3, 5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Goldstein |first=Alan |date=November 11, 1974 |title=2 Broncos thwart Colts |work=The Sun (Baltimore, Maryland) |pages=C5}}</ref> In a September game against the [[1974 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]] that ended in a 35–35 tie, Chavous and teammate [[Bill Thompson (American football)|Bill Thompson]] blocked a 25-yard [[Roy Gerela]] field goal attempt that could have won the game for the Steelers.<ref>{{Cite news |date=September 23, 1974 |title=Pittsburgh And Denver Battle To 35–35 Tie |work=Florence Morning News (Florence, South Carolina) |pages=1B |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

In 1975, Chavous started nine games at left defensive end, with 4.5 sacks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1975 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1975.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was unable to play in five games that season because of a knee injury.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 14, 1975 |title=Sunday Scouting Report |work=The Ogden Standard-Examiner (Ogden, Utah) |pages=7D}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=October 24, 1975 |title=NFL Injury Report |work=The Daily Progress (Charlottesville, Virginia) |pages=B4 |agency=United Press International}}</ref><ref name=":13">{{Cite news |last=MacKay |first=Bill |date=April 27, 1977 |title=Denver Pays Outspoken Visit |work=The Wichita Eagle (Wichita, Kansas) |pages=3B}}</ref> He returned to play all 14 games in 1976, with eight sacks. The Broncos were 9–5 on the season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1976 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1976.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The Broncos defense allowed the sixth fewest points in the NFL that season, and gave up the third fewest rushing yards in the league.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1976 NFL Opposition & Defensive Statistics |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1976/opp.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The Broncos switched to a [[3–4 defense]] in 1976.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jenkins |first=Chris |date=October 15, 1977 |title='Orange Crush' Nickname Doesn't Amuse Swenson |work=Gazette-Telegraph (Colorado Springs, Colorado) |pages=2C}}</ref> Though there would be a number of right defensive ends in the Broncos' three-man defensive line from 1976 to 1985, Chavous was the starting left defensive end and [[Rubin Carter (American football)|Rubin Carter]] was the starting [[Defensive tackle|nose tackle]] for those 10 years.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Rubin Carter Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/C/CartRu20.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> 

In 1977, Chavous was part of Denver's Orange Crush Defense that was ranked first in rushing defense, and set an NFL record in allowing the fewest fourth quarter points.<ref name=":7" /> The Bronco's three-man front line that season included Chavous, Carter and [[All-Pro]] right defensive end [[Lyle Alzado]]. The four starting linebackers included, among others, future Hall of Fame inside linebacker [[Randy Gradishar]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Randy Gradishar Pro Football Hall of Fame profile {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/randy-gradishar |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> and All-Pro outside linebacker [[Tom Jackson (American football, born 1951)|Tom Jackson]].<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":14" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Tom Jackson Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/J/JackTo01.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> 

Chavous started 11 games at left defensive end, with eight quarterback sacks (tied for the team lead with Alzado). Chavous had 51 tackles and 31 assisted tackles during the regular season. The team finished the season 12–2, and made the playoffs for the first time in Chavous's career.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |title=1977 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1977.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=January 15, 1978 |title=Super Sunday, Player Profiles |work=Argus-Leader (Sioux Falls, South Dakota) |pages=2B |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> The Broncos won the [[1977 AFC Championship Game|AFC championship]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=AFC Championship - Oakland Raiders at Denver Broncos - January 1st, 1978 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197801010den.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> and played in [[Super Bowl XII]], losing to the Dallas Cowboys, 27–10. Chavous started the Super Bowl at left defensive end.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XII - Dallas Cowboys vs. Denver Broncos - January 15th, 1978 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197801150dal.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The ''Pittsburgh Courier'' named him Defensive Lineman of the Year.<ref name=":7" />

In 1978, the NFL went to a 16 game schedule.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Koppett |first=Leonard |date=March 30, 1977 |title=N.F.L. Adds 2 Games for Total of 16 in '78 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/03/30/archives/nfl-adds-2-games-for-total-of-16-in-78-nfl-will-expand-season.html |work=The New York Times |pages=A19}}</ref> Chavous started all 16 games for the Broncos at left defensive end for four consecutive seasons, from 1978 to 1981. He had four sacks each of those seasons, except 1980 when he had 4.5.<ref name=":4" /> The Broncos were 10–6 in 1978, and reached the [[1978–79 NFL playoffs|divisional round]] of the playoffs, losing to the eventual [[Super Bowl XIII]] champion [[1978 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]], 33–10.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1978 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1978.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Divisional Round - Denver Broncos at Pittsburgh Steelers - December 30th, 1978 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197812300pit.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XIII - Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Dallas Cowboys - January 21st, 1979 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197901210dal.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The Broncos were 10–6 again in 1979, losing in the [[1979–80 NFL playoffs|wild card playoff round]] to the [[1979 Houston Oilers season|Houston Oilers]], 13–7. Chavous had one sack against Oilers' quarterback [[Dan Pastorini]] in that playoff game, for an 11-yard loss. Pastorini suffered a groin injury on the play, and missed the rest of the game.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1979 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1979.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Wild Card - Denver Broncos at Houston Oilers - December 23rd, 1979 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197912230oti.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=December 24, 1979 |title=Quarterback's Lament |work=The Post (West Palm Beach, Florida) |pages=B5}}</ref>

Chavous played all nine games of the strike-shortened 1982 season, with five sacks. In the season’s last game, he recorded the only [[Safety (gridiron football score)|safety]] of his career against [[Dave Krieg]] of the [[1982 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Denver Broncos at Seattle Seahawks - January 2nd, 1983 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198301020sea.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2007-09-21 |title=Lengthy strike has mostly been forgotten |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/columns/story?columnist=pasquarelli_len&id=3030311 |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1982 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1982.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The Broncos were 2–7 in 1982, but had winning seasons during Chavous's last three seasons, and were in the playoffs twice.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Denver Broncos Team Records, Leaders, and League Ranks |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/index.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Although he suffered a groin injury in 1983, Chavous started 13 games, with two forced fumbles, 4.5 sacks and a fumble recovery.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Spence |first=Mike |date=October 4, 1983 |title=Injuries leave Broncos dependent on rookie line |work=Chieftain and Star-Journal (Pueblo, Colorado) |pages=3B}}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=1983 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1983.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In a November game against the [[1983 Los Angeles Raiders season|Los Angeles Raiders]], Broncos’  linebacker [[Tom Jackson (American football, born 1951)|Tom Jackson]] sacked quarterback [[Jim Plunkett]] and stripped the ball. Chavous recovered the fumble in the endzone for the sole touchdown of his career.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Cox |first=Bob |date=November 14, 1983 |title=Field goal gives win to Raiders |work=The Daily Breeze (Torrance, California) |pages=D1-2}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> The Broncos went 9–7,<ref name=":10" /> losing to the Seahawks in the wild card round of [[1983–84 NFL playoffs|1983–84 playoffs]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Wild Card - Denver Broncos at Seattle Seahawks - December 24th, 1983|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198312240sea.htm|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com|access-date=2026-01-23|language=en}}</ref>

The Broncos were 13–3 in 1984, finishing first in the AFC's West Division. The 33-year old Chavous started 15 games, with 7.5 sacks and one forced fumble.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1984 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1984.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He missed only one game even though he had torn rib cartilage that season.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Socier |first=Dave |date=November 18, 1984 |title=Broncos hope to make Vikes 10th victim in row |work=The Chieftain (Pueblo, Colorado) |pages=4C}}</ref> The Broncos lost to the Steelers in the divisional round of [[1984–85 NFL playoffs|the playoffs]], 24–17. Chavous had a [[Glossary of American football terms|tackle for loss]] during the playoff game.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1984 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1984.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The 1984 Broncos' defense allowed the second fewest points in the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1984 NFL Opposition & Defensive Statistics |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1984/opp.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Although still a starter, he shared time at left defensive end with [[Walt Bowyer]] that season.<ref name=":12">{{Cite news |last=Socier |first=Dave |date=November 3, 1948 |title=Son of Crush |work=The Chieftain (Pueblo, Colorado) |pages=4B}}</ref>

In Chavous's final season (1985), the Broncos were 11–5, but did not make the playoffs. Chavous ended his 13-year Bronco career by starting 15 games with six sacks and one fumble recovery.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1985 Denver Broncos Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/1985.htm |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Chavous announced his retirement in August 1986.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 13, 1986 |title=Transactions, Football, National Football League |work=The Albert Lea Tribune (Albert Lea, Minnesota) |pages=7}}</ref> At the time he retired, Chavous was the Broncos' all-time sack leader.<ref name=":6" /> He ranks fourth on the Broncos' all-time sacks list with 75 (through 2025).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Denver Broncos Career Defense Leaders |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/den/career-defense.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Chavous believed that playing in the [[3–4 defense]] increased the number of double teams from offensive lines that he had to face, and reduced the number of quarterback sacks he could have gotten if he had played more games in a [[4–3 defense]].<ref name=":13" /> 

Chavous started 177 of the 183 games in which he appeared as a Bronco,<ref name=":6" /> and is tied with [[Tom Jackson (American football, born 1951)|Tom Jackson]] for third in Broncos' career starts with 177.<ref name=":7" /> He is also said to have started 178 games.<ref name=":9" /> During his 13-year career with the Broncos, the team only had two losing seasons.<ref name=":6" />
== Coaching career ==
Chavous spent 11 seasons in various coaching roles for the Broncos. He was originally brought in as a coaching intern by head coach [[Dan Reeves]], eventually moving into assistant coaching positions under Reeves and then head coach [[Mike Shanahan]].<ref name=":9" /> He served as an assistant offensive line coach, and strength and conditioning coach under Shanahan. He held those coaching positions at the time the Broncos won [[Super Bowl XXXII]] in 1998 over the [[1997 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]], 31–24; and won [[Super Bowl XXXIII]] over the [[1998 Atlanta Falcons season|Atlanta Falcons]], 34–19.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Low |first=Chris |date=August 11, 1995 |title=No decision in QB battle |work=The Herald (Rock Hill, South Carolina) |pages=4C}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite news |last=Grant Jr. |first=Thomas |date=February 2, 1999 |title=Chavous adds to legacy with second ring |work=The Times and Democrat (Orangeburg, South Carolina) |pages=8A}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XXXII - Green Bay Packers vs. Denver Broncos - January 25th, 1998 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199801250den.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XXXIII - Denver Broncos vs. Atlanta Falcons - January 31st, 1999 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199901310atl.htm |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":9" /> He was later part of the team’s scouting staff.<ref name=":9" />

== Legacy and honors ==
In 1986, Chavous was inducted into the Mid-Eastern Athletic Conference Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Barney Chavous (1986) - Hall of Fame |url=https://meacsports.com/hof.aspx?hof=26 |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=meacsports.com |language=en}}</ref> In May 1998, he was inducted into the South Carolina State University Athletics Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Barney Chavous (1998) - South Carolina State Athletics University Hall of Fame|url=https://www.scsuathletics.com/honors/south-carolina-state-athletics-university-hall-of-fame/barney-chavous/23|website=South Carolina State University Athletics|access-date=2026-01-22|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5" /> He was selected as a member of the Broncos Top 100 Team.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Denver Broncos {{!}} All-Time Top 100 Team |url=https://www.denverbroncos.com/team/broncos100/ |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=www.denverbroncos.com |language=en-US}}</ref> In April 2024, he was inducted into the [[Colorado Sports Hall of Fame]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=DiLalla |first=Arik |date=April 17, 2024 |title=‘It means more to me than I can really express’: Former Orange Crush defender Barney Chavous inducted into Colorado Sports Hall of Fame |url=https://www.denverbroncos.com/news/it-means-more-to-me-than-i-can-really-express-former-orange-crush-defender-barney-chavous-inducted-into-colorado-sports-hall-of-fame |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=www.denverbroncos.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Chavous was known for being softspoken off the field, and for his hard work in physically preparing to play in NFL games, missing very few games over his long career.<ref name=":12" />

==Personal life==
He was a student teacher at [[Holly Hill, South Carolina|Holly Hill]]'s Roberts High School in [[Orangeburg, South Carolina]] as part of his college program at South Carolina State.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":1" /> During his playing days, he was considered religious and family oriented.<ref name=":12" /> Chavous was the head football coach at [[T. W. Josey High School]] in [[Augusta, Georgia]].<ref name=":7" /> Chavous is the uncle of former [[Minnesota Vikings]] [[cornerback]] [[Corey Chavous]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 10, 2015 |title=DraftNasty Showcases Passion of Former Viking DB |url=https://www.vikings.com/news/draftnasty-showcases-passion-of-former-viking-db-15128552 |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=www.vikings.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Now he works as a team sports coach at Tutt Middle school in [[Augusta, Georgia]].{{citation needed|date=January 2026}}
